Abstract. Two disjoint sets of integers greater than one, of cardinalities nine and seven, have equal products of f(t) = Gamma(t+1)/t^t. An explicit prime-valuation certificate proves the identity exactly. This answers negatively the arithmetic question in published Problem 5.6 of On the common transversal probability. A separate Lean certificate proves the literal real Gamma statement.

Aivazidis, Loukaki and Müller [1, Problem 5.6, printed p. 1281] ask whether equality of products of f(t) at distinct integers greater than one forces equal lengths and equality after rearrangement. The published question has no equal-cardinality, equal-sum or group-realization premise. Its preprint number is Problem 12.6. We use the published numbering throughout.
Theorem. Let A = {3,5,6,7,8,14,16,20,36} and B = {4,10,12,15,18,21,32}. These sets are nonempty and disjoint, every entry exceeds one, and
product over A of Gamma(t+1)/t^t = product over B of Gamma(t+1)/t^t.
Since |A| = 9 and |B| = 7, the proposed implication in Problem 5.6 is false.

The witness satisfies both natural readings of distinctness: distinct entries within each list, and all entries distinct across both lists. No minimality, general classification, asymptotic theorem or group realization is asserted.

Theorem 4.6 of [1, pp. 1263-1265] requires one entire side to consist of distinct primes. Both A and B contain composites, so neither orientation satisfies its hypothesis. Its largest-prime and majorization argument depends on that prime-side restriction. Briefly, for L = log N and T the integers up to N with all prime factors at most N/L², a prime-count estimate gives |T| = N - o(N). Small-prime valuation coordinates cost exp(o(N)) possibilities. For larger primes, the factorial valuations are floor(t/p), bounded by L². Concentration confines most subset sums to widths sqrt(N) times powers of log N. Their joint box has exp((1.25506/2 + o(1))N) possibilities, fewer than the 2^(N-o(N)) subsets. Two subsets collide; cancellation gives disjoint supports. This supplies the necessary coefficients in {-1,0,1}; a bare integer kernel would not.
